_comment: Authoring anchors for NEW CED Unit 4 (Inference for Means; OLD topics 5.7-5.8 and 7.x). Describe what DOK-2 and DOK-3 look like here so authors rate by the same yardstick (spec §1.1-1.2). Anchors describe released-FRQ patterns and never quote an item. Mapping/content note: OLD 7.1 carries NEW 4.2 confidence-interval metadata, but its actual legacy framework and worksheet form a VAR-1.I rerandomization-and-error bridge; author 7.1 from that artifact rather than importing OLD 7.2 t-interval mechanics.

dok2_anchors.shape: Given a quantitative population model and sample size, check independence and shape conditions, then calculate the center, standard deviation, z-score, or tail probability for a sample mean or a difference in sample means.
dok2_anchors.why_dok2: The random variable, model, and target probability are supplied, so the student follows a standard condition-and-calculation path without choosing among competing models or claims.

dok2_anchors.shape: Given a named one-sample, matched-pairs, or two-sample t procedure, verify its stated conditions and calculate a standard error, degrees of freedom, interval, test statistic, or p-value in context.
dok2_anchors.why_dok2: Procedure selection and conclusion boundaries are already settled; the student executes and communicates a known multistep algorithm.

dok3_anchors.shape: Two normal models for a sample mean or difference compete; decide which are warranted by population shape, sample size, independence, and standard-error structure, then explain what a rejected approximation would mislead a reader into believing about a tail probability.
dok3_anchors.why_dok3: The student must coordinate multiple routes to approximate normality and separate valid parameter formulas from a potentially invalid shape model; no single calculation resolves the competing claims.

dok3_anchors.shape: Several mean-inference procedures are plausible; select one-sample, matched-pairs, or independent two-sample inference from the study structure and parameter, defend the condition checks, and explain what an alternative analysis would estimate or test instead.
dok3_anchors.why_dok3: The student translates pairing, independence, variables, and the research target into a defensible procedure while tracing the consequence of collapsing pairs or treating dependent measurements as independent.

dok3_anchors.shape: Two students interpret the same mean interval, t-test, or rerandomization result differently; decide which conclusion the uncertainty and design support, distinguish chance probability from certainty or practical importance, and bound causation and population scope.
dok3_anchors.why_dok3: The student coordinates a numerical result, remaining error risk, study design, effect-size claim, and scope of inference to adjudicate competing conclusions and diagnose the overreach.

not_dok3: A longer sampling-distribution, confidence-interval, or t-test calculation after the correct model and procedure have already been named.
A checklist that only compares n with 30 or 10 percent and never asks whether a probability or conclusion remains defensible.
An interval or p-value interpretation prompt that supplies the correct conclusion and asks the student to restate it in context.
Lettered parts that separately calculate, check, and conclude but never adjudicate a model, procedure, interpretation, or scope claim.
Calling any nonzero observed difference in sample means convincing without evaluating how readily random variation could produce it.
